subChunks.title: Stack vs Heap Memory
subChunks.hookHtml: Why does calling a method not corrupt your variables? Why does creating a thousand objects not run out of memory immediately? The answer lies in how Java divides and manages its two main memory regions: the stack and the heap.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Stack Memory

The stack is a LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) structure. It holds:

  • Local primitive variables (int x = 5)
  • Local reference variables (the pointer to an object, not the object itself)
  • Method call frames — when a method is called, a new frame is pushed; when it returns, the frame is popped

Stack access is fast and automatic — the frame disappears when the method ends. Stack memory is limited (typically 512KB–1MB). A very deep recursion causes a StackOverflowError.

Heap Memory

The heap is a larger, unordered region that holds:

  • All objects created with new
  • Arrays
  • String objects (though string literals go in the string pool, a special region of the heap)

Objects on the heap persist until the Garbage Collector reclaims them.

Primitives vs References

int x = 42;               // primitive — value lives on the stack
String s = "hello";       // reference on stack; object on heap
int[] arr = {1, 2, 3};   // reference on stack; array on heap

int a = 10;
int b = a;  // b gets a COPY of 10 — changing b does not affect a
b = 99;
System.out.println(a); // still 10

int[] arr1 = {1, 2, 3};
int[] arr2 = arr1; // arr2 points to the SAME array!
arr2[0] = 99;
System.out.println(arr1[0]); // 99 — arr1 also changed!

This distinction — value semantics for primitives, reference semantics for objects — is one of the most important concepts in Java.

storyBeats.text: Eldrin takes you to the Academy's magical library — two wings, divided by a glass wall. The left wing is tiny but blazingly fast; the right wing is vast but takes a moment to navigate.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The left wing is the stack — small, ordered, lightning-fast. Every time you call a method, a new shelf appears at the top. Local variables are placed on that shelf. When the method returns, the entire shelf vanishes — no cleanup needed.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The right wing is the heap — vast, unordered, holding every object you create with new. The stack holds only a reference — a magical pointer — to the heap object. The object itself lives on the heap until the garbage collector claims it.

storyBeats.speaker: Stack vs heap
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: This creates the most important distinction in Java: value semantics versus reference semantics. Copying a primitive gives you an independent duplicate. Copying a reference gives you a second pointer to the same object.

storyBeats.speaker: The reference trap

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Demonstrate the difference between value and reference semantics:

  1. Declare int p = 5 and int q = p. Modify q to 99. Print p (it should still be 5).
  2. Declare int[] arr1 = {10, 20, 30} and int[] arr2 = arr1. Set arr2[1] = 999. Print arr1[1] (it should be 999 — same array).
  3. Print the result of "hello" == "hello" and of new String("hello") == new String("hello") to see string literal pooling vs heap objects.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between the stack and the heap in Java as if you were teaching a junior developer. Include what types of data go where, and explain the difference between value and reference semantics with a concrete example.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From a blank file, write a reference-semantics investigator:

  • Create a simple class Counter with a public int count field and a no-args constructor that sets count = 0.
  • In main: create Counter c1 = new Counter(). Set Counter c2 = c1. Increment c2.count three times. Print c1.count — it should be 3.
  • Now create Counter c3 = new Counter() (a brand-new object). Increment c3.count twice. Print c1.count again — it should still be 3.
  • Print a sentence explaining what you observe (just a System.out.println with a string literal).

questions.explanationHtml: Objects created with new are allocated on the heap. The reference to the object (the variable) lives on the stack, but the actual object data is on the heap.
Primitives use value semantics — y gets a copy of x's value. Changing y does not affect x.

questions.questionHtml: Two variables reference the same array. If you modify the array through one variable, what happens when you read via the other?
options: The other variable still has the old values
The other variable sees the updated values
A ConcurrentModificationException is thrown
The array is copied automatically
questions.correctAnswer: The other variable sees the updated values
questions.explanationHtml: Arrays are objects stored on the heap. Both variables hold references (pointers) to the same memory. Modifying the array through one reference is immediately visible through the other.

questions.questionHtml: A developer sees this and is confused that the value is unchanged. What is the bug?
questions.correctAnswer: Java passes primitives by value. addFive gets a copy of n; changing that copy does not affect the caller's variable. To return a modified value, the method should return int and the caller should reassign: value = addFive(value);
questions.explanationHtml: Java is always pass-by-value. For primitives, the method receives a copy of the value. Modifications inside the method do not affect the original variable. For objects, the method receives a copy of the reference — you can mutate the object through it, but reassigning the reference variable inside the method does not affect the caller's reference.

subChunks.title: Garbage Collection Concepts
subChunks.hookHtml: In C, programmers manually free memory. Forgetting causes memory leaks. In Java, an automated system called the Garbage Collector handles cleanup — but understanding it prevents subtle performance bugs.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What is Garbage Collection?

The Garbage Collector (GC) automatically reclaims memory occupied by objects that are no longer reachable from any live reference. You never call free() in Java — the JVM handles it.

When is an object eligible for GC?

Wizard w = new Wizard("Lyria", 100); // object on heap, w references it
w = null;                            // w no longer references the object
// the Wizard object is now eligible for GC

// OR: reference goes out of scope
void createWizard() {
    Wizard temp = new Wizard("Temp", 10);
    // temp goes out of scope when method ends — object eligible for GC
}

GC Roots

An object is reachable if there is a chain of references from a GC root to it. GC roots include: local variables on the stack, static fields, and JNI references. Everything else is collectible.

Generational GC

Modern JVMs divide the heap into generations:

  • Young generation — newly created objects (Eden space + Survivor spaces). Most objects die young — GC here is fast.
  • Old generation (Tenured) — objects that survived several young-GC cycles. Collected less frequently.

This matches the observation that most objects are short-lived (e.g., a loop variable, a temporary result).

Avoiding memory leaks in Java

Java can still leak memory if you hold unintended references:

// A growing static list holds references forever
static List<byte[]> held = new ArrayList<>();
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    held.add(new byte[1_000_000]); // 1 MB each — never collected!
}

Always remove references you no longer need: clear collections, close resources with try-with-resources.

Note on finalize(): finalize() is deprecated for removal in Java 21 and must not be used in new code. For deterministic cleanup, implement AutoCloseable and use try-with-resources. For GC-triggered cleanup when try-with-resources is not applicable (e.g. wrapping a native resource), register a java.lang.ref.Cleaner action:

// finalize() is deprecated for removal — use Cleaner instead
private static final java.lang.ref.Cleaner CLEANER = java.lang.ref.Cleaner.create();
private final java.lang.ref.Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;

MyResource() {
    cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, () -> System.out.println("Resource cleaned up"));
}

storyBeats.text: Deep below the Academy, enchanted automata silently patrol the vaults, dissolving conjurations that no wizard is still holding.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Unlike the old days when wizards had to dissolve their own constructs — and some forgot, causing catastrophic overloads — Java employs Garbage Collectors. Any object that no wizard is still pointing to is dissolved automatically.

storyBeats.speaker: Making an object eligible
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The GC finds collectible objects by walking from roots — the live variables on the stack and static fields. Anything reachable is safe. Everything else is claimed.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Java's GC is generational. Most objects are short-lived — a loop counter, a builder, a temporary result. These live in the young generation and are cleared rapidly. Objects that survive long enough are promoted to the old generation, collected less frequently but more thoroughly.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But never be complacent. Even in Java, you can leak memory by holding references you no longer need — a static collection that grows forever, an event listener never deregistered. The GC cannot collect what is still referenced.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
This exercise is observational — we'll demonstrate reachability with a simulation using a simple tracking class.

Write a class TrackedObject with a String label field, a constructor, and a close() method that prints "[label] closed". Use try-with-resources to ensure the object is closed automatically by implementing AutoCloseable.

Note: finalize() is deprecated for removal in Java 21. The modern approach for cleanup actions is to implement AutoCloseable and use try-with-resources, or to register a java.lang.ref.Cleaner action for cases where try-with-resources is not applicable.

In main: use a try-with-resources block to create a TrackedObject named "Alpha" — the close method will be called automatically. Then create TrackedObject b = new TrackedObject("Beta") and print b.label. Finally, print "Done".
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Java's garbage collection to someone coming from a C/C++ background. What does the GC do for you? What can still go wrong? Mention the concept of generational GC.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
From a blank file, write a memory-awareness demonstration:

  • Create a Resource class with a String name. Override toString() to return the name.
  • In main, create a List<Resource> called cache. Add 5 resources with names "R1" through "R5" using a for loop.
  • Print the list size.
  • Remove resources at index 0 and 2. Print the size again.
  • Clear the entire list. Print the size one final time (should be 0).
  • Print the string "Cache cleared — resources eligible for GC".

questions.questionHtml: When does an object become eligible for garbage collection?
options: When the programmer calls System.gc()
When no live references point to it
When the JVM runs out of heap space
After 30 seconds of inactivity
questions.correctAnswer: When no live references point to it
questions.explanationHtml: An object is eligible for GC when it is no longer reachable — no chain of references from any GC root leads to it. System.gc() is only a hint, not a guarantee.

questions.questionHtml: Java's garbage collector guarantees that memory will be freed at a predictable point in time.
questions.explanationHtml: The GC runs at its own discretion, not on a predictable schedule. System.gc() is a hint that may be ignored. You cannot rely on finalize() being called at a specific time.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following can cause a memory leak in Java despite the GC?
options: Using local variables inside a method
Adding objects to a static List and never removing them
Creating objects inside a loop that terminates
Passing objects to methods as arguments
questions.correctAnswer: Adding objects to a static List and never removing them
questions.explanationHtml: A static field is a GC root. Objects held in a static collection remain reachable forever — the GC cannot collect them even if your code never uses them again. This is the most common source of memory leaks in Java applications.

questions.questionHtml: Why does Java's GC use generational collection (young + old generation) rather than a single scan of the whole heap?
options: To support multiple threads
Because most objects die young — frequent short scans of the young generation are cheaper than scanning everything
To support both stack and heap
Java's GC is not generational
questions.correctAnswer: Because most objects die young — frequent short scans of the young generation are cheaper than scanning everything
questions.explanationHtml: Empirical data shows most objects are short-lived (temporary variables, builders, DTOs). Collecting only the young generation frequently is cheap and reclaims the vast majority of garbage. Long-lived objects are promoted to the old generation and collected less frequently, avoiding the cost of scanning stable objects over and over.
